title: The Swapped Camera Lens Behind Digikala's First Web Pages
dek: After a Tehran seller cheated them over a camera, twin brothers built a shop that would not sell a product until it had been properly explained.

story.event: Founding an online electronics shop built on reviews after being cheated over a camera
story.summary: Twin brothers Hamid and Saeed Mohammadi, amateur photographers in Tehran, could find no Persian-language reviews when buying a camera and later found its lens had been swapped by the seller. In 2006 they began building Digikala, a site that paired product information with a shop, and launched it in early 2007 with five staff and their own savings. It took no outside investment for about six years and grew into Iran's largest online retailer.
paragraphs: Hamid and Saeed Mohammadi, twins in their mid-twenties, were Tehran engineers with business degrees and a hobby of digital photography. Around 2005 they set out to buy their first serious camera. "My brother and I were looking to buy one, but we couldn't find a single Farsi review online," Hamid told the BBC in 2015. They chose a Nikon D70 from foreign reviews and found one shop selling it. They later discovered, he told Forbes, that the seller had swapped its lens for a cheaper one. "We spent all our money on that camera. That's how the idea came about."

The idea took shape in the spring of 2006. Phones, laptops and cameras were selling fast, mostly from bazaar stalls offering little information and no returns. A few online shops already existed, and at first Digikala bought from some of them, but Hamid felt their business models were wrong. Neither twin had lived outside Iran, and Hamid said in 2018 that Amazon had not been on their radar. They wanted a site that explained products as well as sold them; both needs, Hamid told Forbes, were "a very real problem for Iranians."

Hamid had worked as a webmaster, and the brothers built the site page by page. According to the technology site Zoomit, it went live early in 2007, run from a small office belonging to their elder brother, with five staff: two content writers, a buyer, an accountant and a courier. A product went on sale only once good content had been written for it. Those pages climbed Google's rankings and the first sale came within weeks. At first the brothers delivered parcels themselves. The starting money was their own: about $10,000, Forbes reported; Saeed later recalled about 20 million toman.

No investor came in for about six years, during which, Saeed said, the company grew by an average of 200 per cent a year. By 2015 the BBC counted 900 staff. The Brandeis economist Nader Habibi told the BBC that sanctions had kept reputable foreign firms such as Amazon and Google out, giving domestic companies room. Saeed saw another side: knowing little of how business worked abroad, he said, spared them noticing many limits. They assumed that whatever they needed, they would have to build.

quote.text: But the man that is just flourisheth; truth goeth in his footsteps, and he maketh habitations therein, not in the dwelling of covetousness.
quote.source_title: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'Gemni, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn, Project Gutenberg eBook #30508
quote.connection: The seller who swapped the lens took a little more than was his. Ptahhotep, in one of the oldest books of advice to survive, says the just man builds his house where truth walks. The twins made a version of that bet in trade: a shop whose first stock was honest information.

reflection: The twins did not begin with a theory of online retail. They began with a particular grievance: a lens swapped by someone who knew more than they did. Much of what Digikala first built, the reviews written before a product could go on sale, the parcels carried by the founders themselves, answers that one moment at a shop counter.

A great deal of useful work starts as a complaint, often your own. The hard part is staying with it long enough to see exactly what went wrong, instead of settling for being annoyed. Some of your clearest thinking may be hidden in the last thing that let you down as a customer, a patient or a colleague.
invitation: Write two lines about the last time you were let down as a customer: what happened, and what precisely would have prevented it. Keep the note somewhere you will find it.

cross_checks.claim: The idea for Digikala came from the brothers' bad experience buying a camera whose lens turned out not to be genuine.
The plan combined product information and reviews with an online shop.
The idea took shape in spring 2006 and the site launched in Bahman 1385 (early 2007).
The brothers started with their own savings and took no outside investment until 2012, growing about 200 per cent a year.
Neither brother had lived outside Iran when they started.

research_notes: Founding date: Wikipedia (not cited) gives 1 July 2006; the brothers told Digiato (2018) that the idea formed at the start of 1385 (spring 2006) and became reality in Bahman 1385 (21 January to 19 February 2007), and Zoomit says the site was born in Bahman 1385. Forbes (January 2015) and the BBC (October 2015) both say 'eight years ago'. The story puts the decision in spring 2006 and the launch early in 2007. Starting money: Forbes says $10,000 of their own savings; Zoomit says 10 million toman (roughly $10,000 at 2007 exchange rates); Saeed told Digiato about 20 million toman. The story gives Forbes's figure and Saeed's recollection side by side. The camera: Forbes says the lens problem appeared a few months after purchase and the seller had swapped it for a cheaper one; the BBC says only that the lens was not genuine; the story says they 'later discovered' the swap. Forbes records Hamid describing the idea as 'a combination of CNET and Amazon', while in 2018 he told Digiato that Amazon had not been on their radar and they had not set out to be an Iranian Amazon; the story uses the 2018 statement and avoids the comparison. The quotation 'a very real problem for Iranians' is from Hamid in Forbes. Persian-language statements (Digiato, Zoomit) are paraphrased in English, not quoted. Sanctions are mentioned only as attributed to the economist Nader Habibi via the BBC and to Saeed's own remark; the story makes no other claim about how sanctions affected the company. The Forbes article is cited from an Internet Archive copy because forbes.com blocks automated requests. Ptahhotep's maxim warns against covetousness; it is applied by analogy to the seller and the shop the twins built.
